fact: CDC says Culex mosquitoes lay rafts of 100 to 300 eggs on the surface of standing water, sometimes in small containers such as buckets, planters, toys, birdbaths and flowerpots, and that an egg takes 7 to 10 days to become an adult mosquito.
quote: Adult female Culex mosquitoes prefer to lay their eggs on the surface of permanent standing water like ponds, edges of lakes, swamps, unmaintained swimming pools, and wastewater treatment plants. … Sometimes they use small containers around the home like buckets, unused tires, planters, toys, birdbaths, or flowerpots. A female Culex mosquito lays eggs one at a time. Eggs stick together to form a raft of 100–300 eggs. The raft floats on the water. A Culex mosquito egg takes 7–10 days to develop into an adult mosquito.
source_label: CDC, About Culex Mosquitoes (Sept. 3, 2025)
notes: cdc.gov returns 403 to plain curl; read in a browser on 2026-09-25 (the old life-cycle URL redirects here). The same page says Culex spread West Nile virus in U.S. states.

fact: CDC says adult Culex mosquitoes are most active from dusk to dawn, rest in grass, shrubs and other thick vegetation that is cool, dark and humid, and have been known to fly up to 2 miles.
quote: Adult Culex mosquitoes are most active from dusk to dawn. … Culex mosquitoes don’t fly long distances but have been known to fly up to 2 miles (3.2 km). … When they are not active, Culex mosquitoes usually rest in grass, shrubs, and other thick vegetation where it is cool, dark, and humid.
source_label: CDC, About Culex Mosquitoes (Sept. 3, 2025)
notes: Read in a browser; cdc.gov returns 403 to plain curl.

fact: CDC advises emptying and scrubbing, turning over, covering or throwing out anything that holds water once a week, including toys, pools, birdbaths and flowerpot saucers, and says mosquitoes rest in dark, humid places such as under patio furniture.
quote: Once a week, empty and scrub, turn over, cover, or throw out any items that hold water like tires, buckets, planters, toys, pools, birdbaths, flowerpot saucers, or trash containers. Mosquitoes lay eggs near water. … Mosquitoes rest in dark, humid areas like under patio furniture or under the carport or garage.
source_label: CDC, Mosquito Control at Home (April 16, 2024)
notes: Read in a browser; cdc.gov returns 403 to plain curl.

fact: CSU Extension says about 40 kinds of mosquitoes occur in Colorado, that adults typically fly a mile or two to feed, and that the kinds expected to spread West Nile virus are most active in July and August.
quote: There are about 3,500 different kinds of mosquitoes. About 40 of these are found in Colorado. … More typically adults will fly a mile or two to feed. … The kinds expected to be important in transmission of West Nile virus are most active during July and August.
source_label: CSU Extension, West Nile Virus and Mosquito Management (reviewed January 2025)
notes: FAQ accordion text; CDPHE's West Nile page links it. The old URL (extension.colostate.edu/topic-areas/insects/west-nile-virus-and-mosquito-management-frequently-asked-questions/) redirects here.

fact: CSU Extension lists heartworm in dogs among Colorado's important mosquito-borne diseases, alongside West Nile virus.
quote: In Colorado, important mosquito borne diseases include West Nile virus, western equine encephalitis, Saint Louis encephalitis, and heartworm in dogs.
source_label: CSU Extension, West Nile Virus and Mosquito Management (reviewed January 2025)

fact: CSU Extension says non-biting midges are the insects most often mistaken for mosquitoes, and that crane flies, which look like very large mosquitoes, develop in damp soils rich in organic matter; neither bites.
quote: The non-biting midges are the insects most commonly mistaken for adult mosquitoes. These may resemble mosquitoes in many features but do not feed on blood and pose no human health risks. … A common group of insects that resemble very large mosquitoes are the crane flies (Tipulidae). These are sometimes called “mosquito hawks”. Both march flies and crane flies develop in damp, organic matter-rich soils. Adults do not bite.
source_label: CSU Extension, West Nile Virus and Mosquito Management (reviewed January 2025)

fact: Larimer County confirmed its first human West Nile case of 2026 on June 25, an adult living in Loveland who may have been infected while traveling, and said the virus is likely circulating in local mosquitoes as it does every summer.
quote: The Larimer County Department of Health and Environment (LCDHE) has confirmed the first reported human case of West Nile virus (WNV) in Larimer County this year. The adult lives in Loveland, however they may have acquired the disease during recent travel to another state. … West Nile virus is likely already circulating in local mosquito populations, as it does every summer.
source_label: Larimer County, first human case of West Nile virus in 2026 (June 25, 2026)
notes: larimer.gov serves a Cloudflare challenge to plain curl; read in a browser on 2026-09-25.

fact: Larimer County's West Nile dashboard reported 5 confirmed human cases and 3 hospitalizations for the 2026 season as of September 23, 2026, and draws a 1-mile radius around each positive mosquito trap as the immediate risk area.
quote: As of September 23, 2026, we are reporting 5 confirmed human cases and 3 WNV related hospitalizations for the 2026 season. … There is a 1 mile radius (highlighted in red) from a mosquito trap which represents the immediate risk of being bitten by a mosquito infected with WNV.
source_label: Larimer County West Nile Virus Surveillance Dashboard (as of Sept. 23, 2026)
notes: Read in a browser (the case graph renders by script). Same page: 6 positive traps of 49 for week 38; the final week of trapping was Sept. 7-11. Update the case count once the season closes.

fact: Larimer County says Colorado's largest West Nile outbreak, in 2003, brought over 2,800 reported cases and 63 deaths, and that infected mosquitoes have been found in the county every year since.
quote: The largest outbreak of West Nile virus in Colorado occurred in 2003, with over 2,800 reported cases and 63 deaths. Some people who became seriously ill are still recovering and some have permanent disabilities. Infected mosquitoes have been found in Larimer County every year since then.
source_label: Larimer County, West Nile Virus
notes: Read in a browser; larimer.gov blocks plain curl.

fact: Larimer County tells residents to drain standing water in their yards at least once a week and to use EPA-registered insect repellent.
quote: Regularly use EPA-registered insect repellent before going outside. … Drain standing water in your yard at least once a week.
source_label: Larimer County, West Nile Virus
notes: Read in a browser; larimer.gov blocks plain curl.

fact: Larimer County says dogs and cats can get West Nile virus from mosquito bites, that most infected pets have mild or no symptoms and recover, and that there is no evidence pets spread it to people.
quote: Pets like dogs, cats, birds, and alpacas can get West Nile virus from mosquito bites. Most pets that get infected with West Nile virus have mild or no symptoms and recover completely. Dead birds do not spread the virus to pets that come into contact with them. There is no evidence that pets can spread West Nile virus to humans.
source_label: Larimer County, West Nile Virus
notes: Read in a browser; larimer.gov blocks plain curl.

fact: Larimer County's list of ways homeowners can help with mosquitoes includes cutting tall grasses, repairing broken sprinkler heads, adding BTI larvicide dunks to standing water the city's contractor doesn't treat, changing birdbath water at least weekly and keeping toys and play equipment from collecting water.
quote: Ensure greenbelts and all common areas have good drainage and tall grasses are cut … Repair broken sprinkler heads … Add larva-killing BTI* granules or “dunks” to standing water in places not treated by the city’s contractor … Change water in birdbaths at least weekly (twice a week in hot weather) … Ensure outdoor toys, playground equipment, and household items don’t collect water
source_label: Larimer County, Mosquito Control Information
notes: The list sits in the collapsed "How Homeowners Can Help" panel; read in a browser (larimer.gov blocks plain curl).

fact: Larimer County runs no mosquito control program of its own: towns such as Windsor, Timnath, Loveland and Fort Collins pay for spraying with the contractor VDCI, residents are asked to report standing water to their town's contact, and an HOA that asks for neighborhood spraying pays for it.
quote: Larimer County does not currently run its own mosquito control program. However, many local municipalities work with Vector Disease Control International (VDCI) to manage mosquito control in their areas. … If you see standing water, please report it to the appropriate contact below, depending on your location. … If an HOA requests spraying, they cover the cost, and we coordinate with them to prevent double spraying in the same area. … For now, mosquito control efforts focus on population centers, and municipalities like Windsor, Timnath, Loveland, and Fort Collins cover the cost of spraying.
source_label: Larimer County, Mosquito Control Information
notes: The page lists a standing-water contact for Loveland, Fort Collins, LaPorte, Timnath, Windsor, Wellington, Berthoud and unincorporated areas. The guide never prints those phone numbers.

fact: Weld County reported its first human West Nile case of 2026 on August 31, a month later than in 2025, after investigating 34 cases in 2025; Culex numbers were below the 5-year average but made up about 80% of trapped mosquitoes, and all three sentinel zones had tested positive.
quote: This is the first case of the 2026 mosquito season in Weld County and comes a month later than in 2025. Last year there were 34 cases of WNV investigated in Weld County. This year, the number of culex mosquitos (those that transmit WNV) trapped is lower than the 5-year average. However, culex mosquitoes are currently making up approximately 80% of mosquitoes that have been trapped in the three sentinel zones in Weld County, which includes the Greeley, Evans, Kersey, LaSalle area, the Johnstown, Milliken, and Platteville area, and the Firestone, Dacono, and Fort Lupton area. These mosquito traps are monitored on a weekly basis and mosquitoes in all three zones have tested positive for WNV.
source_label: Weld County, First positive case of West Nile Virus in Weld County (Aug. 31, 2026)
notes: weld.gov returns 403 to plain curl; read in a browser. The quote names every zone as Weld does; the guide names only the NoCo towns in them.

fact: Weld County's first step against mosquito bites is to drain standing water around the house weekly, from tires, cans, flowerpots, clogged gutters, rain barrels, toys and puddles.
quote: DRAIN standing water around your house weekly. Remember to drain water from tires, cans, flowerpots, clogged rain gutters, rain barrels, toys, and puddles.
source_label: Weld County, First positive case of West Nile Virus in Weld County (Aug. 31, 2026)
notes: Read in a browser; weld.gov blocks plain curl.

fact: Weld County says its mosquitoes are mainly active from June through early September, tells residents to empty week-old water from containers such as toys and pools, and lists 34 human West Nile cases in 2025, 15 in 2024, 52 in 2023, 35 in 2022 and 26 in 2021.
quote: In Weld County, mosquitoes are primarily active from June through early September. … Empty week-old water from tires, buckets, planters, toys, pools, or trash containers. … Weld County Historical Human WNV Cases Year Cases 2025 34 2024 15 2023 52 2022 35 2021 26
source_label: Weld County, West Nile Virus (updated Sept. 9, 2026)
notes: The case counts are a table on the page; the quote runs its cells together. The table also lists 0 in 2020, 9 in 2019, 15 in 2018 and 14 in 2017. Read in a browser; weld.gov blocks plain curl.

fact: Longmont contracts VDCI to spray neighborhoods against West Nile virus, says infected mosquitoes can be found all along the Front Range from mid-June through August, and names birdbaths, clogged gutters and kiddie pools as common breeding sites.
quote: The City of Longmont contracts with Vector Disease Control International (VDCI) to spray Longmont neighborhoods to control the spread of West Nile Virus. … During the peak WNV season (mid-June through August), infected mosquitoes can be found all along the Front Range. … Drain standing water where mosquitoes can breed. Bird baths, clogged gutters and kiddie pools are common breeding sites.
source_label: City of Longmont, Mosquito Control
notes: The breeding-site sentence is in the collapsed "4 D's" panel.

fact: The Colorado health department says the state reported 634 human West Nile cases and 51 deaths in 2023, the most cases in the nation, and advises removing standing water from yards and gutters weekly and treating water that can't be drained with Bti.
quote: Remove standing water from yards and gutters weekly. Treat water that can’t be drained with Bti larvicide. … In 2023, the state reported 634 human cases, including 51 deaths — the highest number of cases in the nation.
source_label: CDPHE, West Nile virus activity confirmed in Colorado, first human cases reported (July 22, 2025)

fact: CSU Extension says huge numbers of ants live on a typical house lot, mostly underground and out of sight, and that ants are on the whole beneficial: they eat other insects, recycle organic matter and aerate soil.
quote: Tremendous numbers of ants normally reside in a typical house lot, although most lead unobserved lives underground or otherwise out of sight. … Overall, the activities of ants are quite beneficial. Many feed on other insects, including pest insects. Ant scavenging helps to recycle organic matter and their tunneling is useful in aerating and mixing soils.
source_label: CSU Extension, Ants in the Home (Fact Sheet 5.518, reviewed August 2025)

fact: CSU Extension says pavement ants pile small mounds of soil at their nest entrances, with nests often under pavement or rocks, and that field ants, common in yards, nest in loose soil.
quote: They characteristically produce small mounds of soil at entrances of their nest, and nests are often located under pavement or rocks … Field ants (Formica species) are often found in yards and gardens … They nest outdoors in loose soil and some produce mounds that incorporate twigs, dried leaves, and other plant materials.
source_label: CSU Extension, Ants in the Home (Fact Sheet 5.518, reviewed August 2025)

fact: CSU Extension says insecticide applied to nests often kills only surface foragers and disturbed colonies move their entrances, while baits usually give the most satisfactory control, take a week or two to show, and lose their appeal when they dry out in Colorado's arid climate.
quote: Similarly, applications of such insecticides made directly to nests will often kill only surface foragers, again providing only temporary control at best. … Where entrance areas are disturbed by insecticides or other activities, colonies will often abandon the treated area and establish new entrances at a different location. … Use of ant baits will usually provide the most satisfactory control. … Baits often become unattractive when they dry out, a common problem in the arid climate of Colorado. … Effects of ant baiting usually start to become apparent within a week or two.
source_label: CSU Extension, Ants in the Home (Fact Sheet 5.518, reviewed August 2025)

fact: CSU Extension says heavy mulch, piled leaves or ground covers against a house can shelter ant colonies, that boiling water carries more hazard than ant insecticides with less chance of success, and that whoever applies a pesticide must follow its label.
quote: Heavy mulch, piled leaves, or ground covers that abut buildings can provide cover for ant colonies and can increase the likelihood of their subsequent occurrence in a house. … Furthermore, the hazards of handling boiling water generally exceed that of using currently available ant insecticides, with less likelihood of success. … It is always the pesticide applicator's responsibility, by law, to read and follow all current label directions for the specific pesticide being used.
source_label: CSU Extension, Ants in the Home (Fact Sheet 5.518, reviewed August 2025)

fact: CSU says fleas are rarely a problem in Colorado's dry climate because cat flea eggs need more than 50% relative humidity to hatch, that the human flea is most often associated with skunks, foxes and coyotes, and that flea larvae stay around host bedding or nests, away from light.
quote: Although rarely observed, flea larvae are worm-like tend to remain around host bedding or nesting sites. … Given Colorado’s dry climate, fleas are rarely problematic. … The most common is the human flea (Pulex irritans), which is most often associated with skunks, foxes, and coyotes. … Eggs of the cat flea require greater than 50% relative humidity to hatch, which limits their ability to reproduce in the dry climate of Colorado. … Larvae tend to move away from sources of light
source_label: Colorado State University, Department of Agricultural Biology, Fleas
notes: The first quoted sentence is verbatim, including its grammar.

fact: CSU Extension says hard ticks climb onto vegetation to wait for a passing animal, are most common at higher elevations and along brushy edges and paths through grass and shrubland, are most active in spring and early summer, and often go dormant in summer heat.
quote: They are particularly common at higher elevations. … When seeking a host, hard ticks will climb onto vegetation. There the tick will remain immobile until a passing mammal signals its presence through vibrations, the warmth of the animal, and the carbon dioxide it exhales. … Survival is shorter under warm, dry conditions and many ticks will go dormant with high temperatures in late spring and summer. … Ticks are most active in spring and early summer and concentrate where their animal hosts most commonly travel. This includes brushy areas along the edges of fields and woodlands or commonly traveled paths through grassy areas and shrublands.
source_label: CSU Extension, Colorado Ticks and Tick-Borne Diseases (reviewed August 2025)

fact: CSU Extension says the Rocky Mountain wood tick is the tick that most often bites people and dogs in Colorado, that the brown dog tick develops only on dogs and is found where dogs are kept together such as kennels, and that the blacklegged tick that spreads Lyme disease does not occur in Colorado.
quote: The most common tick that bites humans and dogs in Colorado is the Rocky Mountain wood tick. … However, brown dog tick develops only on dogs, reinfesting an animal at each stage in its development. Brown dog ticks are more abundant in warmer areas, and in Colorado are found where dogs are present continuously and are kept together in enclosed areas, such as kennels and homes. … The blacklegged tick, the main vector of the organism producing Lyme disease, does not occur in Colorado. … There has never been a confirmed case of Lyme disease originating from a tick-bite in Colorado.
source_label: CSU Extension, Colorado Ticks and Tick-Borne Diseases (reviewed August 2025)

fact: CSU Extension says white grubs and billbugs damage lawns by feeding on grass roots, that native white grubs have long been common in towns along the South Platte River valley, and that raccoons and skunks dig up lawns to find them.
quote: Billbugs and white grubs are insects that damage turfgrasses by feeding on the roots. … White grubs are the most damaging insects that occur in Colorado, and native species have long been particularly common in the TriRiver counties and in towns along the Arkansas and South Platte River valleys. … The presence of white grubs in lawns is also attractive to raccoons and skunks, which will dig up lawns while searching for grubs, often causing more damage.
source_label: CSU Extension, Billbug and White Grub Management in Lawns (reviewed August 2025)

fact: CSU Extension says blow flies commonly breed in carrion or pet waste, and house fly larvae develop in garbage, animal waste and spilled animal feed.
quote: These blow flies are scavengers, particularly of animal-based materials. They commonly breed in carrion or pet waste. … Larvae commonly develop in or near man-made sources of food and can be found in garbage, animal waste, culled fruits and vegetables, and spilled animal feed.
source_label: CSU Extension, Flies in the Home

fact: FieldTurf's maintenance guidelines say spilled sports drinks and other fluids should be rinsed off with water as soon as possible so bugs are not attracted to the turf surface.
quote: We recommend that the areas with Gatorade or other drinks/fluids be cleaned as soon as possible with water in order to avoid bugs being attracted to the surface or jerseys becoming stained as a result of the spilled liquid.
source_label: FieldTurf, Maintenance Guidelines (April 2017)
notes: A sports-field manual (the FAQ "What do I do if we spill Gatorade on the field?"); the page uses it only for what drink spills do on any turf. Read from the PDF with pdftotext on 2026-09-25.
